newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Red Cross suspends operations in Tajikistan.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross suspends operations in Tajikistan.

text.p: The Red Cross said on Thursday it had suspended operations in Tajikistan and sent all non-essential staff to neighbouring Uzbekistan after four United Nations workers were seized in the capital Dushanbe.
The Red Cross retreat came in response to the kidnapping earlier on Thursday of four employees with the United Nations refugee agency, UNHCR, by unknown assailants.

The UNHCR said the agency had had no contact with the four -- an expatriate from Nigeria, a Tajik security guard and two Tajik drivers -- since they went missing in the centre of the capital with two marked U.N. cars.

But U.N. military observers based in Tajikistan said the four were captured by the same armed Tajik rebel group that seized four U.N. military observers -- from Austria, Switzerland and Ukraine -- as well as two Red Cross workers and four Russian journalists.

The U.N. observers said the four had been taken to a place called Obigarm in the central Garm valley about 80 km (50 miles) from Dushanbe in the remote, mountainous Central Asian republic bordering China.
Itar-Tass news agency on Thursday it had received a telephone call from one of the kidnapped reporters, Galina Gridneva, who said that their captors had told them they would be released on Friday.
The others would only be freed if the rebel group won safe passage back into the republic for comrades based in neighbouring Afghanistan, Tass quoted Gridneva as saying.
Both the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and the International Federation of the Red Cross (IFRC) said they had stopped work in the former Soviet republic.
"We have sent all non-essential staff out of the country," said Suzanne Berger, Geneva-based spokeswoman for the ICRC.
"There's no other way out, most of our operations are in the Garm valley," she said. "To send convoys there would be impossible."
Two ICRC members, British national Elizabeth Trinch and her Tajik translator, are among those held hostage.
An official with the IFRC in Kazakhstan told Reuters the organisation had also suspended operations and moved all non-essential staff to Uzbekistan.

The agencies are based in the region to provide aid to the 5.7 million residents suffering hardship brought about by a bitter four-year civil war that has left tens of thousands of people dead and many more homeless.
A ceasefire agreed between the government and the guerrillas has held for nearly two months and further peace talks are due to be held on February 26 in Moscow.

The latest hostage-taking was a setback for embattled Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov, who on Thursday pledged to win the freedom of the journalists and U.N. military observers taken earlier this week.
The hostage-takers are part of a group commanded by Rizyon Sadirov, who used to fight for Tajikstan's Islamic opposition but whose loyalties are now unclear.
"The president held an urgent meeting of the government this morning," presidential spokesman Zafar Saidov said. "He gave them the task of freeing hostages today by peaceful means.

Russian President Boris Yeltsin's spokesman said on Thursday the Kremlin leader was concerned by the hostage-taking and expected all Russian agencies to do "the maximum possible" to ensure the journalists were freed.
